To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
language skill is related to frontotemporal volume in children with epilepsy and in healthy children, but the relationship is different in the two groups.

(i) language skills were associated with gray matter volume in frontotemporal regions in both groups, and with total brain and dorsomedial prefrontal gray/white matter volumes in the controls; (ii) in the epilepsy group, language skills were associated more strongly with gray matter volumes than in the healthy children; and (iii) children with epilepsy who had language deficits had abnormal associations between language and gray matter volumes in brain regions that subserve language.

children with epilepsy with language impairment had abnormal brain volumes and abnormal associations between brain volumes and language skills, while children with epilepsy with typical language scores had brain volumes and associations that were similar to healthy children.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between brain structure and language in children with and without epilepsy.
the development of brain regions involved in language in children with and without epilepsy.
the development of brain and language in children with and without epilepsy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the language skills of children with epilepsy are related to the volume of the brain regions that are involved in language processing, and that the brain reorganization in children with epilepsy differs from that in healthy controls.

children with epilepsy and normal language skills had normal brain volumes and normal associations between brain volumes and language skills, whereas children with epilepsy and language deficits had abnormal brain volumes and atypical relationships between volumes and language.
the brain is a very complex organ, with a very complex network.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
children with epilepsy have abnormal brain volumes and language skills, but those with normal language skills have larger brain volumes than healthy controls.
children with epilepsy with language deficits have atypical associations between brain volumes and language skills.
language deficits are associated with abnormal volumes in the language-related brain regions in children with epilepsy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children with epilepsy with language deficits have abnormal volumes and atypically associated volumes with language skills in frontotemporal regions.
children with epilepsy have smaller brain volumes and that these volumes are associated with language skill.
the relationship between brain volumes and language is not the same in children with epilepsy compared with normal children.
